extracted.intended_audience: judges, attorneys, administrative law practitioners, and scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for when courts should defer to administrative agencies under Chevron (and related refinements) and the criteria for whether entrenched precedent like Chevron should be overruled. Covers Step 1/Step 2 review, exceptions to deference, role of agency expertise, and stare decisis considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A court first determines whether Congress has "directly spoken to the precise question at issue" using all its normal interpretive tools; if Congress has, the court gives effect to that unambiguously expressed intent. But if the statute is "silent or ambiguous" after exhausting traditional tools, the court asks whether the agency's construction is within the sphere of "reasonable" readings—if so, the agency's interpretation controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion frames Chevron as a simple two-part framework: Step 1 (has Congress spoken?) is rigorous; Step 2 (if not) asks only whether the agency's construction is reasonable. Examples illustrating Chevron questions: whether an alpha amino acid polymer qualifies as a "protein" (FDA); what makes a population segment "distinct" (Endangered Species Act); how to define a "geographic area" for Medicare wage adjustments; how to interpret "stationary source" in the Clean Air Act (Chevron itself).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous Step 1 statutory-construction requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: At Step 1 the court must exhaust the "traditional tools of statutory construction" and rigorously determine whether there is a single, unambiguous meaning; if such meaning exists, deference is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1 is characterized as "rigorous": judges must consult text, context, structure, and other ordinary tools. If a court finds a single right answer, "that is the end of the matter." (Kisor/Chevron citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference when statute silent or ambiguous and agency reading is reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after using the court's whole legal toolkit, the statute is still ambiguous or silent on the precise issue, the court should cede primary interpretive responsibility to the administering agency so long as the agency's choice is within a zone of reasonable interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule rests on a presumption of legislative intent that Congress would typically prefer the agency charged with administering the statute to resolve ambiguities. The court remains a backstop policing reasonableness rather than substituting its own policy judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that Congress intends agencies to fill statutory gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron rests on a presumption about legislative intent: when Congress leaves ambiguities or gaps in statutes it enacts, the default presumption is that Congress would want the administering agency—not courts—to exercise interpretive discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is analogous to other judicial presumptions (against extraterritoriality, against retroactivity, against repeal by implication). It is a background rule enabling predictable governance unless Congress clearly indicates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency subject-matter expertise justifies deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Deference is often appropriate because agencies have technical and scientific expertise that courts lack and can bring to bear on specialized statutory questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FDA deciding when a polymer qualifies as a "protein"; Fish & Wildlife Service deciding what makes a population "distinct"; agencies have staff experts and scientific capabilities courts typically lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency operational experience and historical familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's experience implementing a regulatory regime and its historical familiarity with how statutory terms operate across many contexts make its constructions valuable and justify deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency exposure to multiple variations on statutory terms across cases and programs (e.g., prior Species Act determinations, Medicare reimbursement practices) provides comparative and empirical knowledge courts typically do not have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-laden trade-offs are for agencies, not courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory choices that require balancing competing goals, assessing costs and benefits, or making policy trade-offs are more appropriately resolved by agencies than by courts, because agencies are politically accountable and possess domain competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: defining the scope of "natural quiet" over Grand Canyon (noise tradeoffs); choosing plantwide vs device-level definitions of "stationary source" implicates competing regulatory and economic interests. Agencies answer such trade-offs and report to the President who is accountable to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deference when agency does not administer the statute
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency receives no Chevron deference when it is interpreting a statute it is not responsible for administering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis (agency gets no special interpretive role if Congress did not put the agency in charge of the statute). The principle flows from the idea that Congress would not have delegated interpretive primacy to an agency that it did not charge with implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deference when agency fails to use required procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency will not receive Chevron deference for a construction reached without using, or without properly using, the procedures (rulemaking, adjudication) that confer fairness and deliberation to authoritative pronouncements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: United States v. Mead Corp. (importance of procedures), Encino Motorcars v. Navarro. The Court expects authoritative statutory meanings to arise via procedural mechanisms Congress created.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deference for "major questions" of vast economic and political significance
rubrics_metrics.description: In extraordinary cases implicating questions of vast economic or political significance, the court will not defer to an agency construction—Congress would not have left such matters to administrative discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: King v. Burwell. The "major questions" principle limits Chevron where an agency's interpretation would have sweeping effects beyond the ordinary scope of delegated authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts police agencies to ensure interpretations remain within a zone of reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where deference applies, courts have a role: they ensure agencies act within the zone of reasonable options and do not exceed delegated authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court's policing function does not replace agency judgment but constrains it; courts determine when Congress has spoken and whether agency choices are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis: entrenched precedents require particularly special justification to overrule
rubrics_metrics.description: A precedent like Chevron—deeply entrenched and relied upon by numerous governmental and private actors—is entitled to heightened stare decisis protection; overruling it requires a "particularly special justification."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kisor citation and Kagan's dissent stress reliance interests (thousands of judicial decisions, regulatory reliance) and that Congress could have acted to displace Chevron. The majority must justify departure by reference to stare decisis factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors relevant to overruling precedent (workability, reliance, history, rule-of-law values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding whether to discard precedent involves weighing its consistency with statute and administrative law (e.g., APA), historical practices, practical workability, reliance interests, and effects on rule-of-law values such as fair notice and fair hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Gorsuch's concurrence emphasizes Chevron's inconsistency with the APA, historic judicial practice, unworkability in operation, and the undermining of reliance and fundamental rule-of-law guarantees; these are presented as grounds counseling against continued reliance or for overruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Congress has spoken, courts give effect to the unambiguous statutory meaning (text, context, structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statutory text, context, and structure show that Congress has clearly addressed the issue, courts must apply that meaning and not defer to agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kagan cites recent complex decisions resolved by reference to "text," "context," and "structure" (e.g., Becerra v. Empire Health Foundation; Sackett v. EPA; Johnson v. Guzman Chavez) to illustrate courts resolving intricate matters without Chevron deference.
